set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What does trichiasis from trachoma require?
opts: Surgical treatment
Correct — the inturned lashes are the result of fixed cicatricial scarring, which only lid surgery can correct before the cornea is destroyed.
A further course of azithromycin
Antibiotics do not reverse the scarring.
Lubricating drops alone
Insufficient for lashes abrading the cornea.
Observation only
Observation allows the lashes to keep abrading the cornea; lid surgery is needed to prevent blindness.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is emphasised most in evaluating a subconjunctival haemorrhage?
opts: Computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses with contrast
Imaging is not part of this workup.
Immediate slit lamp with fluorescein
Slit lamp with fluorescein looks for corneal epithelial defects; a subconjunctival haemorrhage is diagnosed on inspection and assessed through the history.
Serum lipid profile
That belongs to xanthelasma.
History — and check the blood pressure if there is no explanation
Correct — the eye itself needs little assessment; the value lies in finding a cause, and an unexplained haemorrhage should prompt a blood pressure check.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Preauricular lymph node enlargement in conjunctivitis points to which three causes?
opts: Ordinary bacterial and allergic
Ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis characteristically has NO preauricular node, which is part of what separates it from viral disease.
Fungal and parasitic
Fungal and parasitic organisms are not among the causes of conjunctivitis here; the node points to chlamydial, gonococcal and viral disease.
Chlamydial, gonococcal and viral
Correct — the conjunctiva drains to the preauricular node, and only these three provoke enough lymphoid response to enlarge it palpably.
Allergic, autoimmune and toxic
Allergic, autoimmune and toxic conjunctivitis are not infections and do not enlarge the preauricular node.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is a chalazion, in mechanism?
opts: A sterile obstruction of a meibomian gland
Correct — sterile is the key word separating it from a hordeolum.
An acute staphylococcal infection of a meibomian gland
That is an internal hordeolum.
An acute infection of the glands of Zeis or Moll
That is an external hordeolum.
A lipid deposit in the eyelid skin
That is xanthelasma.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is the definitive treatment for entropion or ectropion?
opts: Long-term lubricating ointment
That is conservative, not definitive.
Botulinum toxin injection
Botulinum toxin does not reposition a lax or scarred lid; surgery is the definitive repair.
Topical antibiotic ointment
Not the definitive treatment.
Surgery
Correct — the lid malposition is mechanical, so only surgical repositioning corrects it definitively.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 13

set1.io: Objective b — Identify medical care strategies for ophthalmological disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations: infant, child, adolescent, adult, elderly
set1.q: Why are neonates with chlamydial conjunctivitis often treated in hospital?
opts: Because the eye disease itself perforates the cornea
That risk belongs to gonococcal disease.
Because intravenous access is required for erythromycin
The regimen is oral.
Because the diagnosis can only be confirmed in hospital
The diagnosis is made from a conjunctival sample that can be taken anywhere; admission is driven by concurrent pneumonia or pneumonitis.
Because there is often concomitant pneumonia or pneumonitis
Correct — the lung involvement is what drives admission.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Which counselling points are attached to doxycycline?
opts: Double the dose if symptoms persist
Doubling the dose is never appropriate self-management; persistent symptoms warrant review rather than more drug.
Avoid the sun, and read which foods cannot be taken with it

Correct — doxycycline is photosensitising and chelates with calcium, iron and magnesium, so sun protection and separating it from antacids and supplements both matter, taken with a full glass of water while staying upright.
Take it on an empty stomach and lie down afterwards
The advice is the reverse: stay upright after the dose, because doxycycline can cause oesophageal ulceration if it lodges on the way down.
Avoid all dairy for a month after the course
The advice concerns timing around supplements, not a month-long ban.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 43

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Which single agent is named that both blocks histamine and stabilises mast cells?
opts: Erythromycin
That is an antibiotic, used in neonatal chlamydial disease.
Doxycycline
That is for adult chlamydial conjunctivitis.
Olopatadine
Correct — olopatadine antagonises the histamine receptor for immediate relief and stabilises mast cells to prevent further release, covering both phases.
Ketotifen
Ketotifen also has dual activity, but olopatadine is the agent named here for that combined action.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 35

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What must happen before immunosuppression in posterior uveitis?
opts: Infection must be excluded
Correct — toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus are among the causes, and immunosuppressing an untreated intraocular infection allows it to destroy the retina.
A lipid profile must be obtained
Unrelated to this decision.
Intraocular pressure must be normalised
Pressure control is not the precondition; excluding an infectious cause before suppressing immunity is.
The patient must have failed topical therapy
Topical therapy does not reach the posterior segment, so failing it is not a meaningful step; excluding infection is what must come first.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 65 (speaker notes)

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: How is acute divided from chronic conjunctivitis?
opts: Acute is 48 hours or less; chronic is longer
Two days is far too short to call anything chronic; the division falls at four weeks.
Acute is three months or less; chronic is longer
Three months is well past the cut-off, which is four weeks.
Acute is four weeks or less; chronic is more than four weeks
Correct — four weeks is the dividing line, and passing it shifts the differential away from ordinary infection towards chlamydial, allergic, toxic and autoimmune causes.
Acute is one week or less; chronic is more than one week
One week is too short; most infective conjunctivitis is still settling then, and the cut-off is four weeks.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 32

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is the mass drug administration regimen for trachoma, and at what prevalence threshold?
opts: Doxycycline 100 milligrams twice daily for seven days, whatever the local prevalence
That is adult inclusion conjunctivitis.
Topical erythromycin to affected individuals only
Treating only the affected individuals leaves the reservoir intact; whole districts are treated once prevalence reaches five per cent.
Azithromycin one gram weekly for four weeks
A single one-gram dose is used; azithromycin's long tissue half-life makes repeated weekly dosing unnecessary.
Azithromycin one gram orally as a single dose, in units with prevalence at or above five per cent
Correct — a single one-gram dose of azithromycin is given to the whole district when prevalence reaches five per cent, since treating individuals alone cannot interrupt transmission.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is the systemic treatment for herpes simplex or zoster keratitis?
opts: Systemic corticosteroids for ten days
Steroids are specifically restricted here.
Oral antivirals — aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir — for ten days
Correct — aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir for ten days treats both, with the valine prodrugs offering better oral absorption and less frequent dosing.
A topical fluoroquinolone given four times daily for ten days
That is chlamydial conjunctivitis.
A topical fluoroquinolone for ten days
That is bacterial conjunctivitis or an ulcer starter.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 59

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is the conservative management, and what should the patient be told about it?
opts: Topical antibiotics for ten days
There is no infection to treat.
Immediate surgical excision in every case
Surgery is indicated only when vision is threatened.
Sun, dust and wind protection with lubricating eyedrops — but it will not make the lesion resolve
Correct — protection and lubrication relieve symptoms and slow progression, but the degenerative tissue is already laid down and will not regress, so expectations must be set.
Sun protection and lubricating drops, which usually resolve the lesion within weeks
Conservative measures relieve irritation and slow growth but do not make the lesion disappear; the deposited tissue does not regress.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 28

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: A mass sits ABOVE the medial canthal tendon rather than below it. What should be suspected?
opts: Orbital cellulitis with proptosis
That produces diffuse swelling and proptosis.
A pterygium
That is a conjunctival lesion at the limbus.
A lacrimal sac tumour, which is rare
Correct — the lacrimal sac lies BELOW the medial canthal tendon, so a mass above it is not a distended sac and raises the possibility of a rare lacrimal sac tumour.
A chalazion
Chalazia sit in the lid, not at the medial canthus.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 24

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Which sign is described at the meibomian glands in meibomitis?
opts: Thick, sometimes toothpaste-like lipid secretion
Correct — inflamed meibomian glands produce inspissated lipid that expresses as a thick, toothpaste-like plug.
Clear watery secretion in excess
The secretion is thickened rather than thinned; a clear watery excess is not the meibomitis finding.
Complete absence of any meibomian secretion
Secretion is present but abnormal; it is thickened and inspissated rather than absent.
Blood-tinged secretion
Blood-tinged secretion is not a feature; the characteristic finding is thick, toothpaste-like lipid.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What happens when the vessels are touched with a cotton-tip applicator after anaesthesia in episcleritis?
opts: They bleed immediately
Bleeding is not a feature; the point of the manoeuvre is that episcleral vessels slide over the sclera while scleral vessels do not.
They can be moved slightly
Correct — mobile vessels mean episcleral, not scleral.
They cannot be moved at all
That is the scleritis finding.
They blanch permanently
Blanching is the phenylephrine test, and it is temporary.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 47

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: How long is lid hygiene given before escalating in blepharitis?
opts: Two weeks
Correct — two weeks of lid hygiene is the trial period before topical antibiotics are added.
Two days
Two days is far too short to judge lid hygiene; the trial runs two weeks.
Two months
Two months is longer than needed; escalation is considered at two weeks.
Six weeks
Six weeks is too long to wait; the trial period is two weeks.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 19

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Which cause of dacryoadenitis is most common?
opts: Fungal
Fungal infection of the lacrimal gland is not a recognised common cause; inflammatory disease is.
Inflammatory
Correct — inflammatory causes predominate, and bacterial infection of the lacrimal gland is rare by comparison.
Bacterial
Bacterial dacryoadenitis is rare; inflammatory causes are much the commonest.
Viral
Viral is listed, and is usually bilateral, but is not named most common.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Which complication follows the outward-turning lid margin of ectropion?
opts: Corneal abrasion from trichiasis
That is the entropion complication.
Sebaceous carcinoma
That is the concern with a recurrent chalazion.
Preauricular lymphadenopathy
Not a complication of ectropion.
Exposure keratopathy
Correct — the lid no longer protects the surface.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is the treatment for dermatochalasis?
opts: Blepharoplasty
Correct — surgical removal of the excess skin.
Lid hygiene twice daily
That is blepharitis management.
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen
That is one of the xanthelasma options.
Warm compresses and massage
That is chalazion management.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Where is the swelling in dacryoadenitis?
opts: Over the nasal aspect of the lower lid
That is dacryocystitis, over the lacrimal sac.
Diffusely across both lids and periorbital tissue
That is cellulitis.
At the lid margin at the lash line
That is an external hordeolum.
Over the lateral one third of the upper lid
Correct — the lacrimal gland sits superotemporally.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: How does the time course of posterior uveitis compare with anterior uveitis?
opts: It always resolves completely within two to three weeks
That is the corneal ulcer healing time.
It develops a lot more slowly and may last several years
Correct — posterior uveitis usually develops far more slowly than anterior disease and can smoulder for years, although some forms are acute and rapidly threaten vision.
It develops faster and resolves within days
Posterior disease is generally the slower of the two and can persist for years rather than resolving in days.
Both follow an identical course
The two differ: anterior uveitis is acute and short-lived, while posterior disease is typically insidious and prolonged.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 65

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What should a patient with a chalazion be told about the timescale of improvement?
opts: It will never improve without surgery
Many chalazia resolve with warm compresses and massage alone; surgery is not inevitable.
Improvement may take months
Correct — a sterile lipid granuloma resolves slowly, and setting an expectation of months prevents premature demands for surgery.
Improvement should be complete within 48 hours
That is the antibiotic response time for cellulitis.
Improvement should be complete within one week
One week is far too fast; a chalazion may take months to settle with conservative treatment.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: When is intravenous aciclovir given in herpes zoster keratitis?
opts: If the patient is immunocompromised

Correct — intravenous therapy is reserved for severe, disseminated, orbital, retinal or central nervous system disease and for significantly immunocompromised patients, rather than for any immune impairment.
In every case of zoster keratitis
Most zoster keratitis is treated orally; intravenous therapy is reserved for severe, disseminated or neurologic disease and significant immunocompromise.
Only if there is a pseudodendrite
The pseudodendrite is the corneal sign, not the escalation trigger.
Only in patients under fifty
Zoster is rarer in the young; age is not the trigger.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 59

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: Which organism most commonly causes acute viral conjunctivitis?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus
That is a bacterial cause.
Adenovirus
Correct — adenovirus accounts for the great majority and explains the highly contagious, watery, follicular picture with a tender preauricular node.
Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex affects the cornea as keratitis with a dendrite rather than causing ordinary acute conjunctivitis.
Chlamydia trachomatis
That is a bacterium and causes a chronic picture.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 36

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is true of the tear film in blepharitis?
opts: It is increased, watery and overflowing
The film is decreased or destabilised rather than increased and watery.
It is unaffected
The tear film is affected; a decreased or frothy film is one of the signs of the disease.
It is purulent
Purulent discharge belongs to bacterial conjunctivitis.
It is decreased, or frothy and foamy
Correct — the disordered lipid layer both reduces tear volume and destabilises the film, so it appears decreased, or frothy and foamy.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What is true of the prognosis of locally treated xanthelasma?
opts: Recurrences are common even after effective local treatment
Correct — local removal clears the deposit but not the metabolic driver behind it, so the lesions commonly return.
Local treatment is curative and recurrence is rare
Recurrence is common rather than rare, because local treatment does nothing to the underlying lipid disorder.
The lesions resolve spontaneously within two to four weeks
That is a subconjunctival haemorrhage.
The lesions progress to sebaceous carcinoma if untreated
That concern belongs to recurrent chalazion.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What causes pinguecula and pterygium?
opts: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
That is dacryocystitis.
Reaction to a systemic allergen
That is allergic conjunctivitis.
Chronic exposure to sunlight and wind
Correct — cumulative ultraviolet light with wind and dust drives degenerative change in the conjunctival stroma, which is why both are commoner near the equator and in outdoor workers.
Colonisation with Staphylococcus aureus
That is blepharitis.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: What separates a pinguecula from a pterygium?
opts: The pterygium is always bilateral
Laterality does not separate them.
The pterygium extends into the cornea; the pinguecula does not involve it
Correct — both are degenerative limbal lesions from chronic exposure, but only the pterygium grows across the limbus onto the cornea, which is what can threaten vision.
The pinguecula extends into the cornea; the pterygium does not
This reverses the two.
The pterygium is yellow and the pinguecula is fleshy
Both are yellowish and fleshy; what separates them is whether the lesion has crossed the limbus onto the cornea.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set1.q: How does xanthelasma appear and how does it feel?
opts: Crusting and scaling around the lash bases
That is blepharitis.
A triangular fleshy wedge growing onto the cornea
That is a pterygium.
Oval-shaped yellowish plaques, and typically asymptomatic
Correct — the lesions are lipid deposits in the dermis, so they form soft yellowish plaques near the medial canthus and cause no symptoms.
Tender red nodules at the lid margin
That is a hordeolum.
set1.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What caution applies before starting corticosteroids in dacryoadenitis?
opts: Do not begin them until bacterial and other infectious causes have been reasonably excluded
Correct — corticosteroids suppress the inflammatory response, so giving them to an undiagnosed bacterial infection allows it to progress.
Do not begin them until a contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan is available
Imaging is not needed in every case; the requirement before steroids is to exclude an infectious cause.
Do not begin them in any patient over sixty-five
Age is not the limiting factor; excluding infection before immunosuppressing is.
Do not begin them without an ophthalmology consultation
Consultation may be helpful, but the specific caution is to exclude bacterial and other infectious causes first.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 23 (speaker notes)

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What is true of the long-term course of blepharitis?
opts: It resolves completely within two weeks of lid hygiene
Lid hygiene improves symptoms but does not cure the disease; it is chronic and needs ongoing control.
It progresses to corneal ulceration if untreated
Corneal ulceration is not the expected course; blepharitis is a chronic lid margin disease controlled with hygiene.
It resolves spontaneously without any treatment
It does not remit on its own; without continued lid hygiene symptoms return.
It is chronic and can be controlled rather than cured
Correct — an important expectation to set with the patient.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: How urgently does a corneal ulcer need ophthalmology?
opts: Emergently
Correct — an ulcer is an established break in the cornea that can perforate, so it goes above the 24-hour urgency of keratitis to emergent referral.
Urgently, within 24 hours
That is the keratitis threshold; the ulcer is emergent.
Routinely
Far too slow.
Non-urgently, if it does not improve in two weeks
Much too slow for sight-threatening disease.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 61

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes cause trachoma, and how does that differ from adult inclusion conjunctivitis?
opts: Both are caused by serotypes A, B and C
The serotypes differ: A, B and C cause trachoma, while D to K cause adult inclusion conjunctivitis and genital infection.
Both are caused by serotypes D to K
D to K cause adult inclusion conjunctivitis; trachoma is caused by serotypes A, B and C.
Trachoma is serotypes A, B and C; adult inclusion conjunctivitis is serotypes D to K
Correct — same organism, different serotypes and different disease.
Trachoma is serotypes D to K; adult inclusion conjunctivitis is A, B and C
This reverses the two.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 45

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Conjunctival FOLLICLES point to which causes?
opts: Autoimmune only
Autoimmune disease is not the follicular group; follicles point to chlamydial and viral infection.
Chlamydial and viral
Correct — follicles are lymphoid aggregates, so they appear where the response is lymphocytic: chlamydial and viral infection.
Bacterial and allergic
Those produce papillae.
Allergic only
Allergic disease produces papillae.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 33

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What is noted about the safety of fluorescein angiography dye?
opts: It contains iodine and is contraindicated in renal impairment
Fluorescein contains no iodine at all, which is precisely what separates it from iodinated radiographic contrast.
It is radioactive and requires shielding
It is not radioactive.
It commonly causes anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis is rare; the usual effects are transient nausea and temporary yellow discolouration of skin and urine.
It is relatively safe and has no iodine
Correct — fluorescein contains no iodine, so the iodinated-contrast precautions do not apply; reactions are usually limited to transient nausea and yellow discolouration of skin and urine.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 10

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which symptom is given for entropion?
opts: Severe boring pain worse at night
That is scleritis.
Itching with stringy discharge
That is allergic conjunctivitis.
Foreign body sensation
Correct — the inward-turned lashes rub the globe.
Tearing
Tearing is the hallmark of ectropion, where the everted lid no longer channels tears into the punctum.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 12

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which laboratory workup is ordered for xanthelasma?
opts: Serum lipid profile, plus tests for diabetes mellitus and liver function
Correct — the plaques are a cutaneous marker of disordered lipid handling, so lipids, glucose and liver function are all checked.
Serum lipid profile alone
A lipid profile alone is incomplete; diabetes mellitus and liver dysfunction also underlie the lesion and are tested for.
Complete blood count with differential, blood cultures and wound Gram stain
That is the cellulitis workup.
Conjunctival nucleic acid amplification testing
That is for chlamydial conjunctivitis.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What is Hutchinson sign and what does it predict?
opts: A violaceous scleral patch, predicting perforation
That is scleritis.
Involvement of the tip of the nose, predicting a higher risk of ocular involvement
Correct — the nasociliary nerve supplies both the nose tip and the globe, so vesicles on the nose tip mean that branch is involved and the eye is at higher risk.
Involvement of the lower eyelid, predicting subsequent corneal scarring
Zoster ophthalmicus often spares the lower lid; it is involvement of the NOSE TIP that predicts ocular disease, through the nasociliary nerve.
A dendrite with end bulbs, predicting recurrence
That is the simplex corneal finding.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 58

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which three associations are given for blepharitis and meibomitis?
opts: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
That underlies dacryocystitis.
Rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis, and colonisation with Staphylococcus aureus
Correct — rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis both disturb the lid margin, and Staphylococcus aureus colonisation completes the triad.
Contact lens wear, dry eye, and chronic topical corticosteroid use
Those are keratitis risk factors.
Chronic sun and wind exposure
That is pinguecula and pterygium.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 18

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Once antibiotics are started for dacryocystitis, when should improvement be expected?
opts: Within 24 to 48 hours
Correct — a soft tissue infection responding to an appropriate antibiotic should be visibly improving within 24 to 48 hours, and failure to do so prompts reassessment.
Within 2 to 3 weeks
That is the healing time for a corneal ulcer.
Within 2 to 4 weeks
That is a subconjunctival haemorrhage resolving.
Within several months
That is chalazion improvement.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: Objective b — Identify medical care strategies for ophthalmological disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations: infant, child, adolescent, adult, elderly
set2.q: Which patients with PRE-septal cellulitis are hospitalised?
opts: Every patient with pre-septal disease, whatever the severity
Mild disease is managed as an outpatient.
Only patients over sixty-five
The age criterion runs the other way: it is children of five or under who are admitted, because spread behind the septum is faster and harder to assess.
Only contact lens wearers
Not a criterion for cellulitis.
Moderate to severe or toxic disease, concern for poor compliance, a child of five years or younger, or no improvement after oral antibiotics were started

Correct — each marks either a patient who cannot be safely observed at home or disease already failing oral therapy, and children of five or under are admitted because post-septal spread is quicker and harder to detect.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 53

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What is true of vision in anterior uveitis?
opts: It is always severely reduced
Vision is often preserved, which is precisely why the pain, photophobia and ciliary flush carry the diagnosis.
It is lost entirely within hours
Vision is typically preserved rather than lost within hours; sudden painful vision loss suggests acute angle closure instead.
It is only affected at night
There is no night-specific pattern; vision is usually preserved, and photophobia is the prominent visual symptom.
It is often preserved
Correct — which is why the other signs matter so much.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 62

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What is the treatment for adult chlamydial conjunctivitis?
opts: Azithromycin one gram orally as a single dose
That is the trachoma mass-treatment dose.
A topical fluoroquinolone for seven days
Topical therapy does not clear the concurrent urogenital infection that accompanies ocular chlamydia, so treatment is systemic.
Doxycycline 100 milligrams orally twice daily for seven days
Correct — doxycycline penetrates cells to reach the intracellular organism, and seven days covers its slow replication cycle.
Erythromycin 50 milligrams per kilogram per day for fourteen days
That is the neonatal regimen.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 43

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Where on the eye do these lesions almost always sit?
opts: Centrally, over the pupil
These are limbal lesions.
At three o'clock or nine o'clock
Correct — the nasal and temporal limbus at three and nine o'clock takes the most reflected sun and wind, which is where the degenerative change occurs.
At twelve o'clock, under the upper lid
The upper limbus is shaded by the lid and brow; these lesions form nasally and temporally at three and nine o'clock.
At six o'clock, on the lower limbus
The lower limbus is not the typical site; exposure is greatest nasally and temporally, at three and nine o'clock.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 27

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: How is an afebrile, systemically well, reliable patient with mild dacryocystitis managed?
opts: Immediate surgical drainage
Incision and drainage is only considered for an abscess.
Outpatient oral antibiotics for ten days
Correct — a well patient with localised infection and reliable follow-up can be treated at home with a ten-day oral antibiotic course.
Hospital admission with intravenous antibiotics for 48 to 72 hours
That is for the febrile, acutely ill or unreliable patient.
Warm compresses alone with no antibiotic
Compresses are adjunctive, not the whole treatment.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which single examination finding separates a chalazion from a hordeolum?
opts: Laterality — the chalazion is always bilateral
Neither is defined by laterality.
Tenderness — the hordeolum is tender and the chalazion is not
Correct — a hordeolum is an acute infection of a lid gland and is tender, while a chalazion is a sterile granuloma of retained lipid and is painless.
Size — the hordeolum is always larger
Size does not separate them; a chalazion can be the larger lesion, and tenderness is what distinguishes them.
Colour — the chalazion is yellow and the hordeolum is red
Colour does not reliably separate them; tenderness does, because only the hordeolum is acutely infected.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What underlies dacryocystitis?
opts: Direct extension from a sinus infection
That is the cellulitis route.
Chronic ultraviolet exposure
That drives pinguecula and pterygium.
Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Correct — obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct dams tears in the lacrimal sac, and the stagnant fluid becomes infected.
Meibomian gland obstruction
That produces a chalazion.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 24

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: How urgently does scleritis need ophthalmology, and why?
opts: Never — scleritis is managed in primary care with lubricating tears
Artificial tears do not treat scleritis; it needs systemic anti-inflammatory therapy and urgent ophthalmology.
Urgently — the sclera is at risk of perforation and may need a surgical patch
Correct — progressive scleral thinning can perforate the globe, which may require a surgical patch graft, so referral is urgent.
Routinely, since it is usually self-limited
Episcleritis is the self-limited one; scleritis threatens perforation and is referred urgently.
Non-urgently, unless vision changes
Referral is urgent whether or not vision has changed, because the risk is scleral perforation.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 50

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which examination behaviour is described in corneal ulcer?
opts: The patient reports no discomfort at all
A corneal ulcer is markedly painful; the cornea is among the most densely innervated tissues in the body.
The patient reports itching rather than pain
Itch points to allergy.
The patient resists opening the affected eye
Correct — photophobia and foreign body sensation make opening the eye painful, so blepharospasm and resistance to examination are themselves a clue.
The patient holds the eye wide open to relieve pressure
The eye is held shut rather than wide open; photophobia and foreign body sensation make opening it painful.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 60

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Beyond local treatment, what should be done for xanthelasma?
opts: Nothing further, since the lesions are cosmetic
They are not merely cosmetic; they mark a metabolic disorder that carries cardiovascular risk.
Start a topical antibiotic
There is no infection to treat.
Refer urgently to ophthalmology
The lesions are not sight-threatening and need no urgent referral; the priority is the metabolic workup.
Treat the underlying metabolic issue
Correct — the plaques signal a lipid or metabolic disorder, so treating that underlying problem matters more than removing the lesion.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: When is a hordeolum referred to ophthalmology, and for what?
opts: Only if the patient also has rosacea
Rosacea matters for recurrence, not for the initial referral.
Never — hordeola are managed entirely in primary care
Persistent lesions are referred; a hordeolum that fails two weeks of conservative treatment needs incision and drainage.
If persistent — for example no improvement in two weeks — for incision and drainage
Correct — a hordeolum that has not improved after about two weeks of warm compresses is referred for incision and drainage.
Immediately at first presentation, for an intralesional steroid injection
Steroid injection or curettage is the chalazion pathway.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which infectious causes are given for posterior uveitis?
opts: Toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus
Correct — toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus both infect the retina and choroid directly, the latter especially in immunocompromised patients.
Adenovirus and Staphylococcus aureus
Those are conjunctivitis causes.
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Those cause conjunctivitis.
Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba
Those cause keratitis.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 64

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which patients carry the greatest perforation risk in scleritis?
opts: All patients with scleritis equally
Risk is not uniform across scleritis; it tracks the necrotising subtype rather than the diagnosis as a whole.
Only patients who also have an identified systemic autoimmune disease
An associated autoimmune disease raises overall severity, but perforation risk follows the necrotising subtype, which can occur without a confirmed systemic diagnosis.
Only contact lens wearers
That risk factor belongs to keratitis.
Those with necrotising disease, rather than all scleritis uniformly
Correct — perforation risk is concentrated in necrotising scleritis, where the sclera is actively destroyed; non-necrotising diffuse and nodular disease carries a far lower risk.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 50 (speaker notes)

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which examination is specified for entropion and ectropion, and what is it looking for?
opts: Slit lamp examination, to assess corneal involvement
Correct — the question is whether the cornea has been damaged.
Computed tomography of the orbits with contrast
That is for cellulitis, dacryocystitis and dacryoadenitis.
Fluorescein angiography
That is used in posterior uveitis and retinal vascular disease.
Serum lipid profile
That belongs to xanthelasma.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 13

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which single risk factor is called major for a corneal ulcer?
opts: Contact lens use
Correct — a contact lens abrades the epithelium and holds organisms against the cornea, which is why lens wear dominates the risk for ulceration.
Sunlight exposure
That drives pterygium.
Hypertension
That is a subconjunctival haemorrhage risk.
Rosacea
That is a blepharitis and chalazion association.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 60

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Why is a chalazion that recurs or persists more than two to three months referred?
opts: To rule out a lacrimal sac tumour
That concern belongs to a mass above the medial canthal tendon.
To rule out sebaceous carcinoma
Correct — sebaceous carcinoma of the meibomian gland can masquerade as a recurrent chalazion, so persistent lesions are biopsied.
To rule out basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is a lid margin tumour, but the malignancy that mimics a recurrent chalazion is sebaceous carcinoma.
To rule out orbital cellulitis
Orbital cellulitis is acute and febrile with restricted eye movement, not a slowly recurring painless nodule.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: Which combination distinguishes acute viral conjunctivitis on examination?
opts: Chemosis and papillae with itching and no node
That is allergic conjunctivitis.
A violaceous scleral hue with deep pain
That is scleritis.
Conjunctival follicles, tender preauricular nodes, and profuse watery discharge
Correct — the lymphocytic response produces follicles, especially inferiorly, and enlarges the draining preauricular node, while the discharge stays watery rather than purulent.
Conjunctival papillae with thick yellow discharge and no preauricular node
That is bacterial conjunctivitis.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: How is INFLAMMATORY dacryoadenitis treated, and how fast should it respond?
opts: Oral antibiotics, with a response expected within 48 hours
Antibiotics are the empiric option when the cause is unclear.
Cool compresses, with resolution over two weeks
Cool compresses are the viral measure.
Intravenous antibiotics for 48 to 72 hours
That is the regimen for severe dacryocystitis or postseptal cellulitis.
Corticosteroids, with a response expected within 48 hours
Correct — inflammatory disease responds to corticosteroids quickly, and a failure to improve within 48 hours should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: Objective a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following common ophthalmological disorders
set2.q: What is true of trachoma's global significance?
opts: It is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide
Correct — repeated childhood infection in endemic areas scars the lids over decades, making trachoma the commonest infectious cause of blindness worldwide.
It is the leading cause of blindness in United States adults over 75
That is macular degeneration, and a different course.
It is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in adults 20 to 74
That is diabetic retinopathy.
It is now eradicated worldwide
Trachoma is targeted for elimination but is not eradicated; mass azithromycin campaigns are still running in endemic districts.
set2.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders 2026 - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 45
